extracted.intended_audience: academic scientists (PIs, postdocs, grad students), NIH-funded researchers, research administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical and career-oriented guidance for academic investigators and their trainees, covering research ethics, publication obligations, mentorship responsibilities, and some regulatory/administrative notes relevant to NIH-funded labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBD scheduling and researcher licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannabidiol is still Schedule I. CBD has been on the Schedule for quite some time and is listed specifically on the application for a researcher license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You won’t be able to buy CBD from a legitimate scientific reagent company (such as Sigma) without a DEA license. DEA clarified that new drug code 7350 for cannabis extracts includes extracts that contain only one cannabinoid; for practical purposes most extracts containing CBD also contain other cannabinoids. Be aware of quack supplement companies importing pure CBD under cover of 'industrial hemp'—this is legally gray and may be subject to prosecution under the new extracts code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed experimental outcomes constitute misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If the lab head tells the trainees or techs that a specific experimental outcome must be generated by them, this is scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lab head says a specific experimental outcome is necessary to publish the paper, this may be very close to misconduct or may be aboveboard depending on context. The recommended context is to cultivate a mantra that any outcome teaches us more about reality and that is the real goal. Note: this guidance excludes routine assay validation/technical development work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to produce publishable results from funded research
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are paid by the taxpayers, or generous private philanthropists, of your country to do science, you owe them a product. If you haven’t published your scientific work, it doesn’t exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should try to publish the work accomplished with other people’s money. When deciding whether to invest additional resources to make partially completed work publishable, weigh the cost of returning to past projects against opportunities for future funding and new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor responsibility: secure first-author publications for trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: The very first rule of PI/mentorship is get your trainees first author publications; this is the thing of biggest lasting career impact that you can determine almost with absolute control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not getting the vast majority of your trainees first-author publications you are failing as a mentor. Have publication plans for all postdocs and later-stage graduate students. Active management is recommended over a 'let the postdoc figure it out' hands-off approach, because failures to publish harm trainees' careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote a lab culture where outcomes (positive or negative) are informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Set a constant mantra that any outcome teaches us more about reality and that is the real goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cultural framing reduces pressure to produce a desired result and helps distinguish acceptable contextual demands (e.g., assay validation) from misconduct (demanding a specific experimental result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary appointment length must reflect work expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are on a '9 month appointment' of Salary X but every workplace expectation is that you will be doing University related work for 12 months, that in fact Salary X is your base 12-month salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are expected to work the extra three months to retain your job or advance (e.g., tenure), treat the appointment as a 12-month job. Selling grant ideas (obtaining summer salary from grants) is an accepted way to compensate for extra months, but be alert to universities using the '9-month' label to underpay for effectively year-round expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of manuscript reviews is flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is totally okay to submit your manuscript reviews earlier than the deadline you have been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor procedural guidance encouraging promptness; no penalty inferred for early submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about publicly criticizing obligated research spending
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaining about a big pile of research funds you 'have to spend out' should be done in highly select company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical/strategic advice: airing such complaints broadly can be unwise—choose audience carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of opportunities and institutional levers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lever of power unexpectedly extends into your operant chamber, press it — take the opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic career advice: use newly available institutional advantages to further your goals; recognize that system dynamics reward those who seize levers of power.
